question: On my first unsecured card bill, should I pay the smaller required amount or the full amount to avoid interest while building credit?
answer: Each month, you'll be issued a statement reflecting both the total balance and the minimum due. Paying your bills on time indicates you are responsible with credit and can help to build your credit score. The minimum payment is the smallest amount you can pay each month without being assessed a late fee. The statement balance, in contrast, is the total amount you spent during the last billing cycle, plus any unpaid balance from previous months. Paying the full statement balance by the due date can help you avoid being charged interest. When you pay this, you will pay off the Pay Over Time plan (and your credit card balance) at that time, which may be earlier than you intended when you set up the plan.

### Unsecured credit cards
An unsecured credit card is—as you may have guessed—the opposite of a secured credit card. An unsecured credit card isn't backed by collateral. Instead, you, as the cardmember, agree to pay back the amount that is charged to the card. Each month, you'll be issued a statement reflecting both the total balance and the minimum due. Paying your bills on time indicates you are responsible with credit and can help to build your credit score.

metadata.heading_path: Statement balance vs minimum payment: What's the difference? > Statement balance versus minimum payment

reference_chunks.content:
## Statement balance versus minimum payment
What is the minimum payment versus the statement balance? The minimum payment is the smallest amount you can pay each month without being assessed a late fee. The amount you see is based on a percentage of your total balance, usually 1-4%.
The statement balance, in contrast, is the total amount you spent during the last billing cycle, plus any unpaid balance from previous months. Paying the full statement balance by the due date can help you avoid being charged interest. Cardholders typically have approximately four weeks from the statement close date to make a payment, and new interest charges aren’t applied to any unpaid balance until after that due date.
Minimum payments are typically the greater of 1–4% of your balance or a fixed amount like $25–$35. For low balances, you’ll pay the full balance if it’s less than the fixed minimum.

## How payments work for Pay Over Time on Amazon
Once a Pay Over Time plan is confirmed, your payment toward it will be added to the minimum amount due on your credit card each month. If you pay at least your minimum payment when it’s due, you’ll typically pay off your plan balance on time. Or, you might choose to pay off the plan by paying your interest saving balance each month and avoid interest on new credit card purchases.
When paying your credit card bill, here’s how each option affects your Pay Over Time plan:
- Interest saving balance: If you normally pay your credit card balance in full to avoid interest, you may choose to pay the interest saving balance payment option. It will tell you exactly what to pay to avoid interest on new purchases and avoid paying off your Pay Over Time plan earlier than intended.
- Minimum payment: If you pay at least your minimum amount due, you’ll typically pay off your Chase Pay Over Time® plan on time. This is because the minimum amount due on your credit card bill each month will be updated to include each installment of a Pay Over Time plan.
- Current statement balance: When you pay this, you will pay off the Pay Over Time plan (and your credit card balance) at that time, which may be earlier than you intended when you set up the plan.

## Maximizing the benefits of using a credit card for home improvement
There are some distinct advantages to financing home improvement projects through a credit card. By leveraging the right credit card, homeowners can not only improve their living spaces but also enjoy a range of financial benefits, making their renovation projects more rewarding and financially manageable Let’s take a close look:
- Timing your purchases: Align your major home improvement purchases with credit card offers such as increased cashback rates or special promotions. This can lead to savings or increased rewards over time.
- Immediate access to funds: Credit cards allow you to begin your home improvement projects immediately, rather than waiting for loan approvals.
- Rewards and cashback: Many credit cards offer rewards points or cash back on purchases, which can be particularly helpful when used for significant expenses like home renovations.
- Purchase protection: Using a credit card often comes with added benefits such as Purchase Protection, Extended Warranties and Return Protection, which can be helpful for large purchases like appliances and tools.
- Special financing options: Some home improvement credit cards offer special financing terms, such as deferred interest periods, which can be a cost-effective way to manage large expenses.
- Building credit: Regularly making timely payments on your credit card can help build your credit score, which could be beneficial for future financial endeavors.
- Utilizing introductory offers: Many credit cards come with special introductory offers, such as signup bonuses or low APR periods. Planning your home improvement projects around these offers could potentially allow you to finance the project without interest during the introductory period and/or to reach the minimum spending limit to earn your signup bonus.
- Combining discounts with credit offers: Look for opportunities to combine store discounts or coupons with the rewards or cash back from your credit card. This double-dip may lead to increased savings.

question: Can I earn portal points if I have a co-branded Chase card and use a promo code not listed after logging in?
answer: The Shops at Chase is an online shopping platform available exclusively to Chase cardmembers. To access The Shops at Chase, securely log in to your account through the official Chase website or Chase mobile app. You should only use discount codes that are provided on the portal because discount codes not available on the portal may disqualify the purchase from earning points. ## How does Shop and Earn work?
To use Shop and Earn, you will need to access the portal by going through either the Chase website or the Chase Mobile® app (more on this later).
From there, you can review brands that are eligible for certain rewards and make your purchase through the portal. Once you find a brand you’d like to shop, click on the retailer/offer through the portal to go to the store’s site.
Your points may be posted to your account on the Shop and Earn shopping details page within 15 days of your purchase, and you’ll receive an email confirming this. However, it can take up to 60 days for the points to get posted to your account.

There are a few important things to keep in mind when making a purchase through the portal:
- If you navigate away from the browser before you make the purchase, it will not count.
- Different Chase credit cards can give different payout rates. You will need to select one during the login process.
- You may not be able to apply gift cards or discount codes on purchases made through the portal. You should only use discount codes that are provided on the portal because discount codes not available on the portal may disqualify the purchase from earning points.
- Rewards earned with co-branded cards cannot be used in the Shop and Earn portal because co-branded cards do not earn Ultimate Rewards points.

question: If I want to keep my low fixed mortgage rate, when would payments on a HELOC start going up?
answer: With a HELOC, you don’t have to refinance to get cash. The repayment period begins once the HELOC draw period ends. Monthly payments will rise because you’re now paying both the principal and the interest.

metadata.page_title: HELOC Draw and Repayment Periods: What Are They? | Chase
metadata.heading_path: What are HELOC draw and repayment periods? > What is the HELOC repayment period?

reference_chunks.content:
## What is the HELOC repayment period?
The repayment period begins once the HELOC draw period ends. It marks the phase when you must start repaying both the principal and the interest. Here are several key details to know:
- No access to funds: You can no longer withdraw funds during the repayment period. Your HELOC is essentially closed, and the focus is on paying down the balance.
- Payment increase: Monthly payments will rise because you’re now paying both the principal and the interest.
- Interest rate adjustment: If your HELOC has a variable interest rate, it may continue to change during the repayment period. Alternatively, you may be given the option to lock in a fixed rate, which can offer stability in your monthly payments.
- Payment schedule: Your lender will set a repayment period for your HELOC, commonly ranging from 10 to 20 years. Along with the interest rate, the length of the repayment period will help calculate a monthly payment. Each payment will cover a portion of both the principal and interest. Following the schedule will pay the amount you borrowed, plus interest, in full.
- Potential for balloon payments: Some HELOCs may require a large “balloon payment” at the end of the repayment period, particularly if only interest was paid during the draw period. However, balloon payments are not standard for all HELOCs; review your loan agreement for specific terms.

### HELOC
This option keeps your current mortgage as is, and, with a new loan, gives you access to cash as needed during the draw period. This may be a good option if your mortgage has a low interest rate.
- Keep your current mortgage interest rate
Currently have a mortgage with a low rate? With a HELOC, you don’t have to refinance to get cash. - Flexibility
Borrow as needed during the HELOC's draw period and spend on what matters most to you. - Lower interest rates
As a HELOC is secured against your home, rates are usually lower than unsecured loans, such as credit cards or personal loans. - Interest-only payments
During the three-year draw period and the following seven years, you’ll make interest-only payments. After that, you’ll have 20 years to repay both principal and interest. Plus, you’re only required to make payments on the amount you actually borrowed. - One-time origination fee upon closing
Pay an origination fee at closing, which will not exceed 4.99% of your total credit limit. This fee is financed into the line of credit.

### The fixed-rate mortgage
The most common type of home loan is the fixed-rate mortgage because the interest rate remains the same for the life of the loan. Fixed-rate mortgages usually last 30 years, though 15 and 20-year loans also are common.
Your monthly payment stays the same with a fixed-rate mortgage, which makes it a great option if you plan to be in your home for many years, especially if interest rates rise. You may pay a slightly higher interest rate on a fixed-rate mortgage than an adjustable-rate mortgage because your interest rate is capped.
